title: Ankylosing Spondylitis (axSpA) | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness, diagnosis, daily exercise, physio and biologic treatment.

What is ankylosing spondylitis? Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), or axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory arthritis mainly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically starts in the late teens or twenties with gradual lower back pain and morning stiffness that improves with movement. Daily exercise, physio and biologic drugs keep the spine flexible.

What is the difference between ankylosing spondylitis and axial spondyloarthritis? Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is the umbrella term. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the form of axSpA where damage to the sacroiliac joints is visible on an X-ray. Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) is the same condition earlier in its course — visible only on MRI. Treatment is the same for both.

What is the first sign of ankylosing spondylitis? The earliest sign is usually persistent lower back or buttock pain that comes on slowly before age 45, is worse in the morning, lasts over 30 minutes and improves with movement.

Is ankylosing spondylitis a disability? AS is recognised under the UK Equality Act 2010 as it can have a long-term substantial effect on daily activities. Many people qualify for reasonable adjustments at work and may be eligible for PIP.

Can ankylosing spondylitis be cured? There is no cure, but biologics, NSAIDs and daily exercise can keep inflammation under control and prevent spinal damage for most people.

What is the HLA-B27 test? A blood test that checks for the HLA-B27 gene, found in around 90% of UK people with AS. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose AS — it's used alongside symptoms and MRI scans.

Should I exercise if my back hurts? Yes — gentle, regular movement is the single most important treatment for AS. Pain that eases with activity is typical. A physiotherapist can build a safe, progressive programme.

title: Elbow Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to elbow arthritis: pain, stiffness, locking and grating in the elbow, with treatments from NSAIDs to arthroscopy and replacement.

What is elbow arthritis? Elbow arthritis is joint damage in the elbow causing pain, stiffness, locking or grating during movement. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are the main causes. Treatment ranges from activity modification and NSAIDs to arthroscopy or elbow replacement.

What does elbow arthritis feel like? Most people describe a deep ache on the outside or back of the elbow that worsens when straightening the arm fully or carrying a heavy bag. Many lose the last few degrees of extension, so the arm no longer goes completely straight.

Is elbow pain always arthritis? No. The most common causes of elbow pain in UK adults are tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) and golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis) — tendon overload conditions rather than joint arthritis. True elbow arthritis is less common and usually follows an old fracture or develops in people with rheumatoid arthritis.

What is the best exercise for elbow arthritis? Gentle range-of-motion work — bending and straightening the elbow within a pain-free range, plus forearm rotations (palm up, palm down) — is the most evidence-supported routine. Light isometric grip work protects forearm strength without loading the joint.

Should I see a GP about elbow pain? See your GP if elbow pain lasts more than six weeks, wakes you at night, locks or catches, or is accompanied by tingling into the ring and little fingers — that pattern can indicate ulnar nerve irritation that benefits from early treatment.

Can elbow arthritis be cured? Arthritis itself isn't cured, but most people manage symptoms well with exercise, activity modification, topical NSAIDs and occasional corticosteroid injections. Elbow replacement is reserved for severe pain or loss of function and gives good relief in around 85% of cases.

title: Fibromyalgia: Symptoms & Management | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to fibromyalgia: widespread pain, fatigue, fibro fog and sleep problems, plus NICE-recommended exercise, CBT and pacing.

What is fibromyalgia? Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and 'fibro fog'. It's a disorder of pain processing rather than joint damage. NICE recommends graded exercise, CBT and paced activity as first-line management.

Is fibromyalgia a form of arthritis? No. Fibromyalgia doesn't damage joints or cause inflammation. However, it commonly occurs alongside arthritis and is treated by similar rheumatology teams.

How is fibromyalgia diagnosed in the UK? Diagnosis is clinical — based on widespread pain lasting over 3 months, plus fatigue, sleep and cognitive symptoms. Blood tests are used to rule out other conditions.

What is fibro fog? Fibro fog is the cognitive symptom of fibromyalgia — short-term memory lapses, word-finding difficulties and trouble concentrating. It improves with better sleep, pacing and exercise.

Can fibromyalgia be cured? There is no cure, but with self-management, exercise, medication and CBT, many people significantly reduce symptoms and stay in work and family life.

Does fibromyalgia get worse over time? Fibromyalgia is not progressive — it doesn't damage tissue. Symptoms fluctuate, often worsening with stress, poor sleep or overdoing activity, and easing with steady self-management.

title: Gout: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to gout: uric acid crystals, sudden severe joint pain, allopurinol treatment after repeat attacks, diet and alcohol changes.

What is gout? Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by high uric acid crystallising inside joints — usually the big toe — triggering sudden severe pain, redness and swelling. UK guidelines recommend urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) after a second attack to prevent joint damage. Diet and alcohol adjustments help.

What are the first signs of gout? The first sign is usually a sudden, severe attack of pain in a single joint — most often the big toe — that wakes you up at night. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even the weight of a bedsheet feels unbearable. Attacks typically peak within 24 hours.

How do I know if my toe pain is gout? Gout in the big toe (called podagra) comes on suddenly, usually overnight, with intense burning pain, redness, heat and swelling at the base of the toe. If you can't bear weight on it or even touch it, and the attack settles over 3–10 days, gout is the most likely cause. A blood test for uric acid and joint fluid analysis can confirm it.

What does a gout attack feel like? Most people describe a sudden, intense burning or throbbing pain in one joint — often the big toe — that starts overnight. The joint becomes red, hot, swollen and so tender that even a bedsheet can be unbearable.

Is gout curable? Gout itself is a long-term condition, but with allopurinol or febuxostat plus diet and lifestyle changes, most people stop having attacks completely.

What foods should I avoid with gout? Limit red meat, organ meats, shellfish, oily fish (anchovies, sardines), beer, spirits and sugary drinks. Cherries, water and low-fat dairy can help reduce attacks.

How long does a gout attack last? An untreated attack peaks at 24 hours and usually settles within 3 to 10 days. NSAIDs or colchicine started early can shorten and ease attacks.

Is gout the same as arthritis? Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric-acid crystals, distinct from osteoarthritis (wear and tear) or rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune).

title: Hand Arthritis: Symptoms & Exercises | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to hand arthritis: finger, thumb and wrist symptoms of OA and RA, plus splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels.

What is hand arthritis? Hand arthritis affects the small joints of the fingers, thumbs and wrists. Osteoarthritis typically causes bony bumps and thumb-base pain; rheumatoid usually causes symmetrical knuckle swelling. Splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels help most people.

What are the first signs of hand arthritis? Early signs include stiffness in the fingers in the morning, a dull ache at the base of the thumb when opening jars or turning keys, and small bony lumps on the end finger joints (Heberden's nodes).

What is the best exercise for arthritic hands? A daily 5-minute routine of fist-to-fan, finger-to-thumb touches, and gentle putty squeezes maintains range of motion and grip strength without overloading inflamed joints.

Do hand splints actually help? Yes — for thumb base (CMC) arthritis, a custom or off-the-shelf neoprene splint reduces pain during pinching tasks and is recommended by NICE as part of first-line care.

Are the bony lumps on my fingers permanent? Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes are bone changes and don't shrink, but the pain associated with their formation usually settles within 1–2 years. The remaining stiffness can be managed with exercise.

When is hand surgery needed? Surgery (most commonly trapeziectomy for thumb base arthritis or joint fusion for severe finger OA) is reserved for persistent pain that hasn't responded to splinting, exercise, injections and topical NSAIDs over 6+ months.

title: Hip Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
content:
UK guide to hip arthritis: groin and buttock pain, stiffness, physio-led strengthening, weight management and hip replacement options.

What is hip arthritis? Hip arthritis is joint damage — usually osteoarthritis — of the hip, causing groin or buttock pain, stiffness and difficulty putting on socks or shoes. Physio-led strengthening, weight management and, when severe, hip replacement (over 100,000 done in the UK each year) provide long-term relief.

What does hip arthritis feel like? Most people feel a deep ache in the groin or front of the hip that worsens with walking, standing up from a chair, or putting on socks. Stiffness is common after sitting and first thing in the morning, usually easing within 30 minutes of moving.

How do I relieve hip pain while sleeping? Sleep on your back or on the unaffected side with a firm pillow between your knees to keep the hips aligned. A medium-firm mattress, a warm bath before bed, and a topical NSAID gel applied to the hip help reduce night pain. Avoid sleeping on the painful side and don't tuck your top knee in front of the bottom one — it twists the joint.

What is the best exercise for hip arthritis? Glute and hip-abductor strengthening (bridges, clams, side-lying leg raises) combined with low-impact cardio such as cycling, swimming or pool walking is the most evidence-based approach. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for everyone with hip OA.

Should I keep walking with hip arthritis? Yes. Regular walking strengthens the muscles that support the hip and reduces pain over time. Build up gradually, wear cushioned shoes, and use a walking pole in the hand opposite to the painful hip to offload the joint by up to 25%.

When is a hip replacement needed? Hip replacement is usually considered when pain disturbs sleep, severely limits walking or daily activity, and conservative measures (exercise, weight management, painkillers, injections) have not worked over several months. UK outcomes are excellent — over 95% of hip replacements still function well at 10 years.

Does losing weight help hip arthritis? Yes. The hip carries roughly three times body weight when walking and up to five times when climbing stairs, so even small weight loss meaningfully reduces joint load and pain.

title: Juvenile Arthritis (JIA) in Children | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to juvenile idiopathic arthritis: signs in children under 16, diagnosis, paediatric rheumatology care and DMARD treatment.

What is juvenile arthritis? Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is arthritis starting before age 16, lasting more than 6 weeks. It affects around 1 in 1,000 UK children. Early paediatric rheumatology care and DMARDs help most children live active lives.

What are the first signs of arthritis in a child? Look out for limping (worse in the morning), a swollen joint, a child avoiding a normally favourite activity, or unexplained fevers and rashes. Always see your GP if joint symptoms last more than two weeks.

Is juvenile arthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis? No. JIA is its own group of conditions. Some forms behave similarly to rheumatoid arthritis, but JIA also includes types not seen in adults, such as systemic JIA (Still's disease).

Will my child grow out of JIA? Some children — particularly those with oligoarticular JIA — do go into long-term remission. Others have ongoing disease into adulthood. Modern treatments have transformed the outlook for most.

Why does my child need eye checks? JIA can cause silent eye inflammation (uveitis) that, if missed, can damage sight. Regular slit-lamp checks by an ophthalmologist are essential.

Can my child still play sport? Yes — sport is encouraged. Swimming and cycling are particularly good. Adapt during flares and work with the rheumatology team and PE staff.

title: Knee Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
content:
UK guide to knee arthritis: pain on stairs and walking, stiffness after rest, NICE first-line exercise, weight loss and treatment options.

What is knee arthritis? Knee arthritis is joint damage in the knee — most often osteoarthritis — causing pain when standing, walking or climbing stairs, stiffness after rest, and swelling. NICE recommends exercise and weight loss as first-line treatment; every 5 kg lost cuts knee load by roughly 20 kg.

What's the best exercise for knee arthritis? Quadriceps strengthening (straight-leg raises, wall sits) plus low-impact aerobic (cycling, swimming). 3-5 sessions a week for 8+ weeks shows meaningful pain reduction.

Should I use a walking stick? Use it in the opposite hand to the painful knee — this reduces load by up to 25%.

title: Lupus (SLE): Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to lupus (SLE): joint pain, butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity, plus hydroxychloroquine treatment and self-care.

What is lupus? Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, heart and lungs. Common symptoms include joint pain, a butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity. Hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay of treatment.

Is lupus a form of arthritis? Lupus isn't classed as arthritis but it commonly causes joint pain and stiffness. Many people are managed by the same rheumatology teams that treat rheumatoid arthritis.

Can lupus be cured? There is no cure, but modern treatments — particularly hydroxychloroquine — control symptoms and reduce flares for most people. Many achieve long periods of remission.

What is the butterfly rash? A flat or slightly raised red rash across the cheeks and bridge of the nose, in the shape of a butterfly. It is one of the most recognisable signs of lupus, though not everyone develops it.

Why is sun protection so important with lupus? UV light can trigger lupus flares — both skin rashes and internal symptoms. Daily SPF 50, UV-protective clothing and hats are essential, even on cloudy UK days.

Can people with lupus have children? Yes. Pregnancy in lupus needs to be planned with your rheumatology and obstetric team, ideally during a period of stable disease, with medications reviewed in advance.

title: Osteoarthritis: Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises | UK
content:
UK guide to osteoarthritis: symptoms, diagnosis, NICE-recommended exercise, weight management, pain relief and when to see a GP.

What is osteoarthritis? Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis in the UK. It happens when protective cartilage on the ends of your bones wears down over time, most often in knees, hips, hands and spine. Symptoms include joint pain that worsens with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, swelling and reduced movement. It's manageable with exercise, weight control, and, when needed, medication or joint replacement.

Can osteoarthritis be reversed? No, cartilage loss can't currently be reversed, but symptoms and progression can be significantly slowed with exercise, weight management and joint-friendly activity.

What's the best exercise for osteoarthritis? Low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming) plus strength training around the affected joint. NICE recommends 30 minutes most days.

Does osteoarthritis show on an X-ray? Yes — X-rays show joint space narrowing and bone spurs, though symptoms don't always match imaging severity.

When should I see a GP? If joint pain limits daily activity, wakes you at night, or hasn't improved after 6 weeks of self-management, book a GP appointment.

title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to polymyalgia rheumatica: sudden shoulder and hip stiffness over 50, low-dose steroid treatment and what recovery looks like.

What is polymyalgia rheumatica? Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) causes sudden shoulder and hip stiffness and pain, mainly in adults over 50. Low-dose steroids (prednisolone 15 mg) usually give dramatic relief within days. Treatment typically continues for 1-2 years.

How is polymyalgia rheumatica diagnosed in the UK? Your GP will check your symptoms, examine your shoulders and hips, and arrange blood tests (CRP and ESR) to look for inflammation. A dramatic improvement within a few days of starting prednisolone helps confirm the diagnosis.

How long does polymyalgia rheumatica last? Most people need steroid treatment for 1 to 3 years. Around half of those affected have one or more flares during the taper, but the condition usually goes into long-term remission.

Is polymyalgia rheumatica an autoimmune disease? Yes — PMR is driven by an overactive immune response that inflames the lining of joints and bursae, particularly in the shoulders and hips. It is not contagious and is not caused by anything you have done.

What is the link with giant cell arteritis? Around 1 in 5 people with PMR also develop giant cell arteritis (GCA), which inflames blood vessels in the head. New headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or any change in vision need urgent medical attention.

Can I exercise with polymyalgia rheumatica? Yes, and you should. Gentle walking, shoulder and hip mobility work, and light resistance training protect muscle and bone during long-term steroid use. Start slowly and build up.

Are there natural alternatives to steroids for PMR? There is no proven natural alternative to steroids for PMR — untreated inflammation can damage tissue and increase the risk of GCA. A Mediterranean diet, exercise and bone-protection medicines support steroid treatment rather than replace it.

title: Psoriatic Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to psoriatic arthritis: the link between psoriasis and joint inflammation, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and self-care.

What is psoriatic arthritis? Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that affects around 1 in 5 people with psoriasis. It causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — often in fingers, toes, lower back or knees — plus nail changes and skin plaques. Early diagnosis and DMARDs or biologics prevent joint damage.

Can you have PsA without psoriasis? Yes, about 15% of people develop joint symptoms before skin symptoms. Family history and nail pitting are clues.

Is psoriatic arthritis worse than rheumatoid arthritis? Both can cause serious joint damage. PsA has more variable patterns; RA is usually more symmetrical. Outcomes depend on early treatment.

title: Reactive Arthritis: Causes & Recovery | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to reactive arthritis: joint inflammation after gut or urinary infection, typical symptoms, treatment and recovery timeline.

What is reactive arthritis? Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body — usually gut or urinary. Symptoms include joint pain, eye inflammation and urinary symptoms. Most cases resolve within 3-12 months.

How long does reactive arthritis last? Most people recover fully within 3 to 6 months. Around 1 in 5 develop longer-lasting joint problems, and a smaller number go on to develop a chronic inflammatory arthritis, which is why early specialist input matters.

Is reactive arthritis curable? Yes — for most people reactive arthritis settles completely once the triggering infection clears and inflammation is treated. NSAIDs, joint injections and physiotherapy speed recovery.

Can reactive arthritis come back? It can. People with the HLA-B27 gene are more likely to have repeat episodes, often triggered by a new gut or urinary infection. Practising food hygiene and safer sex reduces the risk.

How is reactive arthritis diagnosed in the UK? Your GP will ask about recent gut, urinary or chest infections and examine your joints, eyes and skin. Blood tests (CRP, ESR, HLA-B27), urine tests and sometimes joint fluid analysis or imaging are used to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other arthritis.

Is reactive arthritis contagious? No. Reactive arthritis itself cannot be passed from person to person. However, the infections that trigger it (such as chlamydia or salmonella) can be — so treating partners and practising good food hygiene matters.

What is the difference between reactive arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis? Reactive arthritis is triggered by a recent infection, usually affects one or a few large joints, and most people recover within months. Rheumatoid arthritis is a lifelong autoimmune disease that typically affects small joints on both sides of the body and needs long-term medication.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to rheumatoid arthritis: early signs, symmetrical joint symptoms, DMARD treatment, diet support and living well with RA.

What is rheumatoid arthritis? Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of your joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness — usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet). Early treatment with DMARDs (disease-modifying drugs) within 3 months of symptoms starting can prevent joint damage. It affects about 400,000 adults in the UK.

Is rheumatoid arthritis a disability? It can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it substantially affects daily activities. Many people with RA are eligible for PIP.

What's the difference between OA and RA? OA is wear-and-tear cartilage loss. RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease. RA usually affects joints symmetrically and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour).

Can diet help RA? A Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, olive oil and vegetables can reduce inflammatory markers. It doesn't replace DMARDs but supports overall control.

title: Shoulder Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
content:
UK guide to shoulder arthritis: glenohumeral and AC joint OA, night pain, reduced reach, physio, injections and replacement options.

What is shoulder arthritis? Shoulder arthritis is cartilage loss in the glenohumeral or acromioclavicular joints, causing deep aching pain, reduced reach and night pain when lying on the affected side. Physio, corticosteroid injections and, if severe, shoulder replacement are options.

What does shoulder arthritis feel like? Most people describe a deep ache at the back of the shoulder that worsens when reaching overhead, behind the back, or lying on that side at night. Stiffness limits putting on coats and reaching seatbelts.

Is shoulder arthritis the same as a frozen shoulder? No. Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is inflammation of the joint capsule and usually resolves within 1–3 years. Shoulder arthritis is cartilage wear and is progressive — but both can cause similar early symptoms, so accurate diagnosis matters.

What is the best exercise for shoulder arthritis? Pendulum swings, doorway stretches and gentle external rotation with a resistance band are the most evidence-supported exercises. They protect range of motion and rotator cuff strength without overloading the joint.

Should I get an injection in my shoulder? Corticosteroid injections can give 6–12 weeks of meaningful pain relief and are useful to bridge a flare or to allow physiotherapy to progress. Most clinicians limit injections to 2–3 per year.

When is shoulder replacement needed? Shoulder replacement is considered when night pain is severe, function is limited despite physiotherapy and injections, and X-rays confirm advanced joint changes. The reverse total shoulder replacement is the most common option in the UK.

title: Diet & Nutrition Hub for Arthritis | UK
content:
The best diet for arthritis: Mediterranean eating, anti-inflammatory foods, weight loss guidance and UK supermarket-friendly meal plans.

What's the best diet for arthritis? A Mediterranean diet — oily fish twice a week, olive oil, nuts, wholegrains, plenty of vegetables and fruit — consistently reduces inflammation markers and joint pain in trials. Cut ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks and excess red meat. Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.

title: Exercise Hub: Arthritis-Friendly Workouts | UK
content:
Free arthritis exercise hub: aerobic, strength and flexibility routines by joint, NICE-aligned plans and short home video sessions.

What's the best exercise for arthritis? Combine aerobic (walking, swimming, cycling) with strength training 2-3 times a week and flexibility work. NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise as first-line for all arthritis types — with pain reduction comparable to NSAIDs and no side effects.

title: ACR20/50/70: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Trial-outcome measures for RA improvement. ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50%...

What is acr20/50/70? ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50% or 70% in RA trials. Used to compare drugs but rarely quoted directly in NHS clinics.

title: ACT: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain. ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses...

What is act? ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses on living well with pain rather than eliminating it. Growing NICE endorsement for chronic primary pain. Available via NHS Talking Therapies.

title: Acupuncture: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Traditional practice sometimes used for chronic pain. Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points.

What is acupuncture? Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points. NICE no longer recommends it for OA (evidence downgraded), but some people find it helpful for chronic pain as part of a broader plan. Rarely available on NHS for arthritis.

title: Adalimumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
An anti-TNF biologic (brand Humira). Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions.

What is adalimumab? Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions. Self-injected every 1-2 weeks. Biosimilars are widely used in the NHS. Screening for TB, hepatitis and current infections is essential before starting.

title: Allopurinol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The main long-term urate-lowering drug for gout. Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks.

What is allopurinol? Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks. Started at low dose after the acute attack settles, titrated up over months. Target: uric acid <360 μmol/L, or <300 with tophi.

title: Amitriptyline: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A low-dose antidepressant used for pain and sleep. Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain...

What is amitriptyline? Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain including fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain. Improves sleep and reduces pain sensitivity. Not addictive but takes weeks to work.

title: Ankylosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Fusion of bones in a joint. Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous.

What is ankylosis? Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous. Untreated inflammation and immobility promote it. Prevention through medication and exercise is far more effective than reversal.

title: Anti-CCP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A more specific blood test for rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid...

What is anti-ccp? Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for diagnosing RA. Positive anti-CCP predicts more aggressive disease and helps rheumatologists decide on early aggressive treatment.

title: Arthrodesis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Surgical joint fusion. Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain.

What is arthrodesis? Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain. Sometimes done in ankles, wrists, spine and small joints when replacement isn't suitable. Trades movement for pain relief.

title: Arthroscopy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Keyhole surgery to look inside a joint. Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint.

What is arthroscopy? Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint. Small incisions, thin camera. NICE no longer recommends 'clean-out' arthroscopy for OA — evidence showed no benefit — but it remains useful for specific mechanical problems.

title: Attendance Allowance | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A UK benefit for people over State Pension age with a care need. Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over...

What is attendance allowance? Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of illness or disability. £68.10-£101.75/week (2025 rates). Doesn't require an assessment of ability to walk.

title: Biologic: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Injected/infused drug targeting a specific part of the immune system. Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs...

What is biologic? Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs alone don't control inflammatory arthritis. UK NICE approves them based on disease activity scores. Examples: adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab, rituximab. They increase infection risk so vaccinations and screening are essential.

title: Bisphosphonates: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Drugs that slow bone loss. Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk...

What is bisphosphonates? Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk in osteoporosis. Weekly tablet or annual infusion. Take on an empty stomach, stay upright 30 min. Rare jaw and thigh bone side effects.

title: Blue Badge: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
UK parking concession for people with severe mobility problems. Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with...

What is blue badge? Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with severe walking difficulty. Automatic eligibility with higher-rate PIP mobility; discretionary applications also possible. Fee £10 in England, free in Wales/Scotland.

title: BMI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Body mass index, a rough weight-for-height measure. BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared.

What is bmi? BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. Rough guide only — doesn't distinguish muscle from fat. NHS categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 healthy, 25-29.9 overweight, 30+ obese.

title: Bone density (BMD) | Arthritis Glossary
content:
How mineral-dense your bones are. Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score.

What is bone density (bmd)? Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score. Below -1: osteopenia; below -2.5: osteoporosis. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D and, when needed, bisphosphonates maintain BMD.

title: Bone scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Nuclear medicine test for bone activity. Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone.

What is bone scan? Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone. Used for detecting metastases, hidden fractures, complex regional pain syndrome and bone infections.

title: Capsaicin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A chilli-derived topical pain cream. Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application.

What is capsaicin? Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application. NICE-recommended for OA hand and knee. Available on NHS prescription. Wash hands after use.

title: Cartilage: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Smooth tissue covering the ends of bones in a joint. Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet...

What is cartilage? Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet in joints. It cushions impact and allows friction-free movement. In osteoarthritis, cartilage gradually thins and roughens; it has no direct blood supply so heals slowly.

title: CBD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Cannabidiol — a cannabis compound used for pain. CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement.

What is cbd? CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement. Evidence for arthritis pain relief is preliminary. Legally sold if <0.2% THC. Not the same as prescribed medical cannabis.

title: Clinical Frailty Scale | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A 9-point score used by NHS staff. Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill).

What is clinical frailty scale? Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Used across the NHS in hospital admissions and community care. Scores 1-3 fit; 4-5 vulnerable; 6+ frail.

title: Codeine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A mild opioid painkiller. Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol).

What is codeine? Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol). Constipation is universal; addiction risk with regular use. NICE increasingly cautions against long-term opioid use in chronic non-cancer pain.

title: Colchicine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A drug for acute gout attacks. Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable.. Effective if started early in the attack.

What is colchicine? Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable. Effective if started early in the attack. Dose reduced from historical high doses because of side effects.

title: Corticosteroid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Anti-inflammatory drug given as tablet, injection or infusion. Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly...

What is corticosteroid? Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly reduce inflammation but have long-term side effects: weight gain, high blood sugar, bone thinning, mood changes. Used short-term for flares or as targeted joint injections.

title: Crepitus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The grating or crackling sound in a moving joint. Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves.

What is crepitus? Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves. Common in OA and often harmless in isolation — many people over 40 have crepitus without pain. Concerning if painful or new.

title: CRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
C-reactive protein — a faster blood marker of inflammation. CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation.

What is crp? CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. Rises faster than ESR (hours vs days) and drops more quickly when inflammation resolves. Used to monitor flares and treatment response in inflammatory arthritis.

title: CT scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Computed tomography — detailed bone imaging. CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images.

What is ct scan? CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images. Better than plain X-ray for complex fractures and bony detail; poorer than MRI for soft tissue. Uses ionising radiation.

title: Dactylitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Sausage-like swelling of an entire finger or toe. Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined...

What is dactylitis? Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined joint and tendon inflammation. Highly characteristic of psoriatic and reactive arthritis. Requires rheumatology assessment.

title: DAS28: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A score for measuring RA disease activity. DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment...

What is das28? DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment escalation. Combines tender joints, swollen joints, ESR/CRP and patient global rating. NICE thresholds determine biologic eligibility.

title: DAS28 remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A DAS28 score under 2.6 indicating minimal RA activity. DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission.

What is das28 remission? DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission. Achievable in around half of people on early aggressive treatment. Goal of modern RA management.

title: DASS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale. DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress.

What is dass? DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress. Used to identify mental health impact of chronic conditions like arthritis. NHS Talking Therapies uses similar tools to guide treatment.

title: DEXA scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The standard test for bone density. DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine.

What is dexa scan? DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine. Standard test for osteoporosis diagnosis. Low radiation dose. NHS available on GP or specialist referral.

title: DMARD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug — slows joint damage in inflammatory arthritis.

What is dmard? DMARD: DMARDs are drugs that slow the underlying disease process in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, JIA). Conventional DMARDs include methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide. Starting a DMARD within 3 months of RA symptoms significantly reduces long-term joint damage. All require regular blood monitoring.

title: Enthesitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone.

What is enthesitis? Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone. Characteristic of spondyloarthropathies (AS, PsA) and often the first symptom (e.g. Achilles tendon pain, plantar fasciitis).

title: Epidural: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Injection of drugs into the spinal space. Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root...

What is epidural? Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root pain). NICE recommends caution — some benefit for acute severe sciatica, limited role in chronic back pain.

title: Erythema migrans: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A characteristic rash of Lyme disease. Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease.

What is erythema migrans? Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease. Antibiotics started early prevent Lyme arthritis and other complications. If you develop joint pain after a tick bite and rash, see your GP promptly.

title: ESR: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate — blood test for inflammation. ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating...

What is esr? ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating inflammation. Elevated in inflammatory arthritis, infections, and other conditions. Used alongside CRP to monitor disease activity, not for diagnosis alone.

title: Etanercept: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
An anti-TNF biologic (brand Enbrel). Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly.

What is etanercept? Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly. Widely used in the UK for RA, PsA, AS and juvenile arthritis. NHS eligibility depends on disease activity scores (DAS28).

title: Facet joint injection | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Steroid injection into small spine joints. Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the...

What is facet joint injection? Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the back of the spine. Used for suspected facet-mediated back pain. Evidence for lasting benefit is mixed.

title: Falls risk: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Likelihood of falling in the next year. Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and...

What is falls risk? Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and vision. Assessed via history (previous falls, near-falls), timed-up-and-go test, and medication review. Halveable with structured intervention.

title: Flare: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A period when arthritis symptoms suddenly worsen. Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling...

What is flare? Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling and fatigue — lasting days to weeks. Common triggers: stress, illness, over-exertion, weather changes, missed medication. Have a written flare plan agreed with your rheumatology team.

title: Frailty: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A state of reduced reserve and resilience. Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to...

What is frailty? Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to setbacks. Assessed with tools like the Clinical Frailty Scale. Reversible early: strength training, protein, treating cataracts, medication review.

title: FRAX score: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A tool that estimates 10-year fracture risk. FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and...

What is frax score? FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and major fracture based on age, sex, BMI, family and clinical factors. Used by NHS GPs to decide who needs bone-density scanning or treatment.

title: Gabapentin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Related nerve-pain medication. Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia).. Also a controlled drug in the UK.

What is gabapentin? Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia). Also a controlled drug in the UK. Cheaper than pregabalin. Titrated up over weeks; withdrawal must be gradual.

title: Gout attack: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A sudden onset of severe joint pain from urate crystals. Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the...

What is gout attack? Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the big toe. Peaks within 24 hours. Treated with NSAIDs, colchicine or short steroid course. Recurrent attacks need urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol).

title: GP referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
When your GP refers you to a specialist. GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon).

What is gp referral? GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon). For MSK physio, many areas now allow self-referral without GP. Waiting times for rheumatology first appointment: 4-30 weeks depending on area.

title: Hip replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Surgery to replace a worn-out hip joint. Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic...

What is hip replacement? Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic components. Around 100,000 done in the UK yearly. Excellent outcomes for pain and function; modern implants last 20+ years for most.

title: HLA-B27: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A gene marker linked to inflammatory spinal arthritis. HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but...

What is hla-b27? HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but also in ~8% of the general UK population without disease. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose disease — clinical assessment and imaging are essential.

title: Hydrotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Exercise in a heated pool for pain relief and mobility. Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C).

What is hydrotherapy? Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C). Water reduces joint load and warmth eases pain, allowing movement that isn't possible on land. NHS access varies; some rheumatology units offer courses.

title: Hydroxychloroquine | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A DMARD often used in mild RA and lupus. Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy.

What is hydroxychloroquine? Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy. Requires annual eye checks because of a small long-term retinal risk. Safe in pregnancy.

title: NHS Talking Therapies | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Free NHS psychological therapy. NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy...

What is nhs talking therapies? NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy for adults with anxiety, depression and chronic pain. Self-referral online in most areas. Waiting times variable.

title: Infliximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
An anti-TNF biologic given by infusion. Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks.

What is infliximab? Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks. Used in RA, PsA, AS, Crohn's and other conditions. Requires ongoing hospital appointments but effective and predictable.

title: JAK inhibitor: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A newer oral targeted arthritis drug. JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune...

What is jak inhibitor? JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune signalling pathway. Highly effective in RA and PsA. UK regulators have restricted use in some groups because of cardiovascular and cancer safety data.

title: Joint effusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Fluid build-up inside a joint causing swelling. Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing...

What is joint effusion? Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing visible swelling, tightness and reduced movement. Common in OA, RA, gout, trauma or infection. May be drained (aspirated) to relieve symptoms and analyse the cause.

title: Kinesiology tape: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Elastic tape applied to joints for support. Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without...

What is kinesiology tape? Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without restricting movement. Evidence for specific pain relief is limited, but many people report benefit as part of a broader rehab plan.

title: Knee replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Surgery to replace part or all of a worn knee. Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces.

What is knee replacement? Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces. Total knee replacement is more common than partial. Recovery: hospital stay 1-3 days, walking with aid within weeks, full recovery 6-12 months. Physio before and after is critical.

title: Labrum: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Cartilage rim of the hip or shoulder socket. Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and...

What is labrum? Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and helping stability. Tears can cause pain and clicking. Some are surgically treated but many respond to physiotherapy.

title: Leflunomide: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A conventional DMARD used in RA and PsA. Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective.

What is leflunomide? Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective. Requires regular blood monitoring and effective contraception in men and women (long half-life).

title: Medical cannabis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Prescribed cannabis-based products in the UK. Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely...

What is medical cannabis? Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely prescribed for arthritis — usually reserved for specific licensed conditions (severe epilepsy, chemotherapy nausea, MS spasticity).

title: Meniscus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Cartilage disc in the knee that cushions the joint. Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint.

What is meniscus? Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint. Age-related tears are common and often symptomless. NICE recommends physiotherapy first for degenerative tears — surgery only for specific mechanical symptoms.

title: Methotrexate: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The most common first-line DMARD. Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken...

What is methotrexate? Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken once weekly with folic acid on other days. Requires regular blood tests. Common side effects (nausea, tiredness) often improve after a few months.

title: Morning stiffness | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Joint stiffness first thing after waking. Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis.

What is morning stiffness? Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis. Stiffness over an hour, especially symmetrical, points to inflammatory arthritis like RA and needs urgent GP review. Duration is a key diagnostic clue.

title: Morphine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A strong opioid, rarely used long-term in arthritis. Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for...

What is morphine? Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for long-term benefit is poor and risks (dependence, falls, respiratory depression) are high. Occasionally used short-term for severe flares or post-op.

title: MRI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Magnetic resonance imaging — detailed joint imaging. MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail.

What is mri? MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail. Best for cartilage, ligaments, tendons and early inflammatory changes not visible on X-ray. No radiation. NHS waiting times vary.

title: Musculoskeletal (MSK) | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Related to muscles, bones, joints, tendons and ligaments. Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints...

What is musculoskeletal (msk)? Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints, tendons or ligaments. MSK conditions are the leading cause of work absence and disability in the UK, affecting around 20 million people. Most GP visits for back pain, joint pain and sports injuries are MSK.

title: NICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The UK body that publishes health guidance. NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the...

What is nice? NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the NHS in England (and adopted by Wales/NI). Key arthritis guidelines: NG226 (OA), NG100 (RA), CG79 (RA in adults). Your care should broadly follow NICE guidance.

title: NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (e.g. ibuprofen, naproxen). NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with...

What is nsaid? NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with sustained use. NICE recommends topical NSAIDs first for hand/knee OA. Take with food; check with pharmacist if over 65, taking blood thinners, or with kidney/heart conditions.

title: Topical NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
NSAID applied as gel or cream to the skin. Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint.

What is topical nsaid? Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint. NICE first-line for hand and knee OA — comparable pain relief to oral NSAIDs but far lower systemic risk.

title: Occupational therapy | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Practical help adapting daily activities to your condition. Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities —...

What is occupational therapy? Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities — dressing, cooking, work, hobbies — using adapted techniques, aids and equipment. NHS OTs assess your home and provide equipment such as grab rails free of charge.

title: Orthotics: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Shoe inserts to redistribute foot and joint load. Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the...

What is orthotics? Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the foot, ankle, knee and hip. Helpful for hallux valgus, flat feet, plantar fasciitis and some knee OA. NHS podiatry can prescribe them.

title: Osteophyte: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A bony spur that grows near an arthritic joint. Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by...

What is osteophyte? Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by osteoarthritis. Show clearly on X-rays. They can restrict movement and, in the spine, sometimes press on nerves — but many are painless.

title: Osteoporosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Low bone density that increases fracture risk. Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens.

What is osteoporosis? Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens. Screening after menopause or long-term steroid use. Managed with lifestyle, calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonates (alendronic acid) if high risk.

title: Osteotomy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Surgery to reshape bone around an arthritic joint. Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint.

What is osteotomy? Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint. Sometimes used in younger patients with unilateral knee OA to delay replacement. Now less common with modern replacement techniques.

title: Otago exercise programme | Arthritis Glossary
content:
An NHS-endorsed strength and balance course. Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg...

What is otago exercise programme? Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg strength and balance exercises. Randomised trial evidence shows ~35% fewer falls in older adults. Available through NHS falls services.

title: Pain scale (0-10) | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Numeric rating of pain intensity. Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time.

What is pain scale (0-10)? Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time. 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable. Useful for consultation, less useful for diagnosis (subjective).

title: Pannus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Inflamed tissue that invades and damages joints in RA. Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes...

What is pannus? Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes that erode cartilage and bone. Early effective DMARD treatment prevents pannus formation and the resulting joint damage.

title: Passive vs active movement | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Someone moves your joint for you vs you move it yourself. Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its...

What is passive vs active movement? Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its range without you contracting muscles. Active movement is when you do it yourself. Both are used in arthritis rehabilitation — passive keeps joints supple; active builds strength.

title: Physiotherapy triage | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Assessment to decide the right care pathway. Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in...

What is physiotherapy triage? Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in general practice) to sort MSK problems into: self-management, physio treatment, imaging, or specialist referral. Reduces GP burden and speeds care.

title: PIP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Personal Independence Payment, a UK disability benefit. PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term...

What is pip? PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Assessed on functional impact, not diagnosis. Arthritis frequently qualifies; Citizens Advice offers free application help.

title: Pregabalin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A drug for nerve pain and fibromyalgia. Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia.

What is pregabalin? Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. Controlled drug in UK — slow to increase, slow to reduce. Side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dependence risk.

title: Prolotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Injection of irritant solutions to promote healing. Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to...

What is prolotherapy? Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to stimulate healing. Evidence is preliminary and mixed. Not routinely available on NHS. Sometimes offered privately for chronic joint pain.

title: Proprioception: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The body's sense of where its joints are. Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking.

What is proprioception? Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking. Arthritis and joint injury impair proprioception, worsening balance and falls risk. Specific balance and coordination exercises restore it.

title: PRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Platelet-rich plasma injections. PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing.

What is prp? PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing. Evidence for arthritis is emerging but not strong enough for routine NHS use. Common in private sports medicine.

title: Radiofrequency denervation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Nerve ablation for chronic back pain. Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal...

What is radiofrequency denervation? Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal facet joints. Considered by NICE for carefully selected patients with confirmed facet-joint pain who haven't responded to other treatments.

title: Range of motion (ROM) | Arthritis Glossary
content:
How far a joint can move in each direction. Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation.

What is range of motion (rom)? Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation. Physiotherapists compare your ROM to normal ranges and track improvement. Regular gentle movement preserves ROM even in painful joints.

title: Raynaud's phenomenon | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Fingers/toes turning white and blue in the cold. Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then...

What is raynaud's phenomenon? Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then red. Primary Raynaud's is common and benign. Secondary Raynaud's is linked to autoimmune conditions (scleroderma, lupus) and needs specialist review.

title: Remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
When arthritis symptoms are absent or minimal. Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers.

What is remission? Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers. In RA, drug-induced remission is now a realistic goal with early DMARDs. Medication is usually continued even during remission to prevent flares.

title: Rheumatoid factor | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A blood antibody found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of...

What is rheumatoid factor? Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Can also be positive in other conditions (Sjögren's, chronic infections) and in ~5% of healthy older adults, so it's diagnostic only with symptoms.

title: RICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation for joint injuries. RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression...

What is rice? RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Recent evidence (PEACE and LOVE) suggests early gentle movement may be preferable to prolonged rest, but RICE remains a useful starting point.

title: Rituximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A biologic that targets B-cells. Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months.

What is rituximab? Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months. Used when TNF-blockers fail or aren't suitable. Requires screening for hepatitis B and monitoring for infection risk.

title: Sarcopenia: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake.

What is sarcopenia? Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake. Reversible with resistance training and adequate protein (~1.0-1.2 g/kg/day). Contributes to falls and frailty.

title: Self-referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Booking NHS physiotherapy without a GP appointment. Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter.

What is self-referral? Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter. Common for MSK physiotherapy, IAPT/Talking Therapies and sexual health. Search 'NHS [service] self referral [your area]'. Saves both your and your GP's time.

title: Septic arthritis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Bacterial infection inside a joint — a medical emergency. Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain...

What is septic arthritis? Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain, swelling, redness, warmth and fever. Requires emergency hospital treatment: joint drainage and IV antibiotics. Delay can destroy the joint within days.

title: Seronegative: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Arthritis with negative blood tests for RA antibodies. Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or...

What is seronegative? Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or anti-CCP tests. Includes AS, PsA, reactive arthritis. Diagnosis relies on clinical picture and imaging; management is similar to seropositive disease.

title: Shared decision-making | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Doctors and patients agreeing treatment together. Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options...

What is shared decision-making? Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options and patients contribute values and preferences to reach a treatment plan. Especially important in arthritis where multiple options fit different lifestyles.

title: Sjögren's syndrome | Arthritis Glossary
content:
An autoimmune condition causing dry eyes and mouth. Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks...

What is sjögren's syndrome? Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and mouth. Often coexists with RA and lupus. Managed with tear substitutes, saliva stimulants and immunosuppression when needed.

title: Spinal fusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Surgery joining two or more vertebrae together. Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain.

What is spinal fusion? Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain. Considered for specific structural problems (severe instability, deformity). Not a routine treatment for chronic non-specific back pain.

title: Stem cell therapy | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Experimental cell-based treatments. Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental.. Regulatory framework is tight.

What is stem cell therapy? Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental. Regulatory framework is tight. Beware of overseas clinics making strong claims. UK approved treatments are limited to specific research settings.

title: Subchondral bone: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
The bone just underneath the joint cartilage. Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage.

What is subchondral bone? Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage. In OA, it thickens ('sclerosis'), may develop small holes ('cysts') and gets damaged as cartilage thins. Changes are visible on X-ray and are diagnostic.

title: Sulfasalazine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A conventional DMARD. Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies.. Taken as tablets.

What is sulfasalazine? Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies. Taken as tablets. Common in the UK because it's affordable and safe in pregnancy (unlike methotrexate). Can cause harmless orange discolouration of urine and skin.

title: Synovium: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Thin lining of a joint that produces lubricating fluid. Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule.

What is synovium? Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule. It produces synovial fluid, which lubricates and nourishes cartilage. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the synovium, causing swelling, warmth and long-term joint damage.

title: TENS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for pain relief. TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain...

What is tens? TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain signals. Available from pharmacies for £20-50. Evidence in chronic arthritis pain is modest but many people find them helpful, with no side effects.

title: Tocilizumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A biologic that blocks IL-6. Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis.

What is tocilizumab? Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis. Available as subcutaneous injection or IV infusion. Requires regular blood monitoring.

title: Tophi: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Chalky uric acid deposits under the skin in chronic gout. Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or...

What is tophi? Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or joints in long-standing gout. They cause deformity and joint damage. Their presence means urate-lowering therapy is essential.

title: Tramadol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A moderate-strength painkiller. Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain.

What is tramadol? Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain. Interacts with many antidepressants and can lower seizure threshold. Long-term use in chronic pain is discouraged by current NHS guidance.

title: Triple therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Combining three DMARDs in rheumatoid arthritis. Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an...

What is triple therapy? Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an evidence-based combination for people with RA whose disease isn't controlled on methotrexate alone. Cheaper alternative to biologics with comparable outcomes for some patients.

title: Ultrasound: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Real-time imaging of joints and soft tissue. Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real...

What is ultrasound? Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real time. Increasingly used by rheumatologists for early RA detection and injection guidance.

title: Uric acid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
A waste product that forms crystals in gout. Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown.

What is uric acid? Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown. High blood levels ('hyperuricaemia') can crystallise in joints, causing gout attacks. Managed by lowering intake (alcohol, offal, seafood) and, when attacks recur, urate-lowering drugs (allopurinol).

title: Uveitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Eye inflammation associated with inflammatory arthritis. Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred...

What is uveitis? Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred vision. Strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies. Any red painful eye with AS needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.

title: Weight loss for arthritis | Arthritis Glossary
content:
Losing weight to reduce joint load. Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.

What is weight loss for arthritis? Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain. Every 1 kg lost cuts knee load by about 4 kg during walking. Combine with strength work to protect muscle mass.

title: Arthritis Pain Relief: What Works | UK Guide
content:
Evidence-based arthritis pain relief for UK patients: paracetamol, topical NSAID gels, heat and cold, exercise, injections and DMARDs.

How do I relieve arthritis pain? First-line pain relief includes paracetamol, topical NSAID gels and heat/cold packs. Exercise reduces pain more than most drugs long-term. If pain persists, your GP can consider oral NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections or, for inflammatory arthritis, DMARDs.

title: Arthritis vs Fibromyalgia | UK Comparison Guide
content:
Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-proc...

How do I know if it's arthritis or fibromyalgia? Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-processing condition — pain and tenderness spread across the body, plus fatigue, poor sleep and 'fibro fog', with normal joint examination and imaging. It's common to have both. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is clinical, based on ACR criteria.

When would you pick Arthritis? Localised joint pain; visible swelling; imaging changes; morning stiffness in specific joints.

When would you pick Fibromyalgia? Widespread body pain; tenderness on touch; fatigue; sleep issues; 'fibro fog'.

What should I be careful about? Both respond to graded exercise, sleep hygiene and CBT — different medications from your GP.

title: Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
content:
A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affect...

Do I qualify for a Blue Badge with arthritis? A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affects walking.
